\section*{Limitations}

Our primary evaluation uses WikiText-2 perplexity, and downstream benchmarks reveal that perplexity is a poor proxy for reasoning ability at moderate sparsity: 40\% sparsity achieves PPL 8.36 but MMLU already degrades, motivating 30\% as the recommended operating point for downstream fidelity.
Training requires 1000 steps on WikiText-103 ($\sim$45 minutes on RTX PRO 6000 for KL, $\sim$17 minutes for BCE), but a separate predictor must be trained for each sparsity target.
Our recommended operating point (30\% sparsity, uniform allocation) is validated at 7--8B scale; at 14B, the MMLU gap persists regardless of allocation strategy (\S\ref{sec:14b}). Scaling to 70B remains untested.
Out-of-distribution evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}) covers 30\% and 50\% sparsity on C4; extending to 70\% is left to future work.
Our attribution of KL's advantage to gradient coupling (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}) is supported by SNR measurements and the BCE isolation ablation, but does not fully disentangle coupling from oracle quality: BCE uses magnitude-based oracles while KL directly optimizes output preservation, and an ablation using KL-derived masks as BCE targets would more precisely isolate the coupling effect.
At 30\% sparsity, global allocation exhibits 9.5pp cross-seed MMLU standard deviation (3-seed); allocation strategy interacts with predictor initialization in task-specific ways. This variance is MMLU-specific, as ARC, WinoGrande, and GSM8K show stable performance across seeds under both allocation strategies.
While we motivate our work with inference speedup potential, actual wall-clock acceleration depends on sparse kernel implementations (e.g., Triton, cuSPARSE) and hardware-specific memory access patterns; this work focuses on prediction quality rather than systems optimization.
Future directions include N:M structured sparsity for hardware-native acceleration, scaling to 13B+ models, and training a single predictor that serves multiple sparsity targets simultaneously.

\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
This suggests KL should outperform BCE under global allocation.
The empirical picture, however, reveals something more fundamental: KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 53\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 47\%), and a causal ablation confirms that these learned mask patterns, not gradient coupling, are the primary quality driver.
BCE trained on KL-derived targets recovers KL-level perplexity (9.29 vs.\ 9.21, $\Delta$=0.08), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.92 at 50\% sparsity (3-seed); under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL).
At the recommended 30\% operating point, global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), motivating uniform allocation for deployment.
Evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} and Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} confirms the PPL advantage at 7--14B, though 14B exhibits an MMLU gap (63.7\% vs.\ TEAL's 71.8\%) not resolved by allocation strategy.
Our contribution targets prediction quality and inference simplification; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns diverging 53\% from magnitude-based masks. A causal ablation proves that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, determines quality under global allocation (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).
\item These superior mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels, yielding a simpler inference pipeline (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
This suggests KL should outperform BCE under global allocation.
The empirical picture, however, reveals something more fundamental: KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 53\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 47\%), and a causal ablation confirms that these learned mask patterns, not gradient coupling, are the primary quality driver.
BCE trained on KL-derived targets recovers KL-level perplexity (9.29 vs.\ 9.21, $\Delta$=0.08), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.92 at 50\% sparsity (3-seed); under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL).
At the recommended 30\% operating point, global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), motivating uniform allocation for deployment.
Evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} and Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} confirms the PPL advantage at 7--14B, though 14B exhibits an MMLU gap (63.7\% vs.\ TEAL's 71.8\%) not resolved by allocation strategy.
Our contribution targets prediction quality and inference simplification; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns diverging 53\% from magnitude-based masks. A causal ablation proves that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, determines quality under global allocation (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).
\item These superior mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels, yielding a simpler inference pipeline (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}

To understand \emph{what} the KL predictor learns, we compare KL-derived masks against magnitude-based oracle masks (the BCE training targets) at 50\% sparsity on WikiText-2.
Per-layer Jaccard similarity between the two mask types averages 47\% across 32 layers: the KL predictor discovers a neuron importance ranking that diverges 53\% from activation magnitude.
Despite this divergence, KL achieves PPL 11.79 vs.\ BCE's 28.13$\pm$0.20, confirming that output-distribution fidelity, not magnitude agreement, determines mask quality under global allocation. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, bce50_3seed, c1_mask_overlap

\paragraph{Causal Ablation: Target Quality vs.\ Gradient Coupling.}
To disentangle whether KL's advantage stems from its coupled gradient pathway or from the mask patterns it discovers, we train a standard BCE predictor on KL-derived oracle masks instead of magnitude-based masks.
Under controlled evaluation (TEAL 50\% uniform allocation at matched sparsity), BCE trained on KL targets achieves PPL 11.96, identical to the KL predictor (11.96); gradient coupling contributes exactly zero PPL improvement.
Standard BCE on magnitude masks yields PPL 28.13$\pm$0.20 (3-seed, Table~\ref{tab:main}), $2.4\times$ worse.
Mask target quality is the sole driver: when given KL-discovered targets, BCE's factorized gradient recovers equivalent performance.
The coupled gradient is a means to discover better targets, not an independent source of quality. % exp_id: c1_bce_kl_targets_teal50u, bench_kl50_uniform, bce50_3seed

Since BCE on KL targets matches KL exactly, one might consider a two-stage pipeline (train KL, extract oracle masks, retrain with BCE).
This offers no practical advantage: the final BCE predictor equals the KL predictor in performance while adding an extra training phase; the KL predictor already produces contextual per-input masks directly.

\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
This suggests KL should outperform BCE under global allocation.
The empirical picture, however, reveals something more fundamental: KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 53\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 47\%), and a causal ablation confirms that these learned mask patterns, not gradient coupling, are the primary quality driver.
Under controlled 50\% evaluation, BCE trained on KL-derived targets exactly matches KL perplexity (both 11.96), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.92 at 50\% sparsity (3-seed); under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL).
At the recommended 30\% operating point, global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), motivating uniform allocation for deployment.
Evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} and Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} confirms the PPL advantage at 7--14B, though 14B exhibits an MMLU gap (63.7\% vs.\ TEAL's 71.8\%) not resolved by allocation strategy.
Our contribution targets prediction quality and inference simplification; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns diverging 53\% from magnitude-based masks. A causal ablation proves that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, determines quality under global allocation (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).
\item These superior mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels, yielding a simpler inference pipeline (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}
